summary:
Orbis is a lunar mission planning application that helps people explore, evaluate, and compare potential landing sites near the moon's south pole.

Choosing a landing site involves finding the right terrain, and finding the right balance between sunlight and visibility to earth. Steep areas or craters can make power generation hard, complicating mission safety.

Orbis tackles these challenges by combining NASA lunar terrain datasets with NASA/JPL SPICE astronomical data in a single, and co-operative workspace, so a team can share ideas, and find the optimal spot together. Users can analyze sun and earth visibility over time, and try to find an appropriate window if the current one isn't optimal with our tool.

The 3D terrain vizualization tries to give the user an idea of their landing spot candidate. There is also a small interactive tour, showing ten spots with a short description and image for each.
details:
Orbis combines NASA lunar terrain datasets with NASA/JPL SPICE astronomical data. Users can work together, select locations, define mission parameters, and evaluate candidate regions.

Orbis' benefits are bringing terrain exploration, candidate searching, and analysis into one interactive and co-operative experience.

We want to make lunar mission planning concepts more accesible to students, educators, researchers and space enthusiasts.

We used React, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS for the frontend.

For the backend we used Python, FastAPI and SQLite.

NASA LOLA terrain datasets and NASA/JPL SPICE kernals are used.

Orbis is creative because it combines geographic and astronomical data into an interactive workflow that allows users to explore different locations, dates, mission parameters and see what could affect potential landing-sites.

We considered sunlight availability, communication with earth, terrain slope, roughness, arrival dates, data resolution, and landing-site estimates.
